description: What is a cell in a spreadsheet?
explanation: A cell is the single box where one row and one column meet, and it is identified by its column letter and row number.
choice1: The box where a row and a column meet
choice2: A saved copy of the file
choice3: A group of selected rows

description: What does the reference B4 point to?
explanation: A reference names the column letter first and the row number second, so B4 is column B, row 4.
choice3: Columns B through 4

description: How does every formula in a spreadsheet begin?
explanation: A formula starts with an equals sign. Without it the cell is treated as plain text.
choice3: With the word FORMULA

description: What is a worksheet, sometimes called a tab?
explanation: A worksheet is one grid of cells inside a workbook, and a workbook can hold many of them.
choice0: A printed copy of the data
choice3: One grid of cells inside a workbook

description: What does the range reference A1:A5 describe?
explanation: A colon defines a range covering every cell from the first reference to the second, here five cells in column A.
choice0: Cells A1, A2, A3, A4 and A5
choice2: The result of A1 divided by A5
choice3: The five sheets named A1 to A5

description: Which formula adds the values in cells A1 through A10?
explanation: SUM adds every number in the range it is given.
choice3: =PLUS(A1:A10)

description: Which function returns the arithmetic mean of a range?
explanation: AVERAGE adds the numbers and divides by how many there are.
choice3: =MEDIAN(B1:B9)

description: Which function returns the largest value in a range?
explanation: MAX returns the highest number found in the range.
choice3: =HIGH(C1:C20)

description: Which function returns the smallest value in a range?
explanation: MIN returns the lowest number found in the range.
choice3: =MIN(C1:C20)

description: What does =COUNT(A1:A10) return?
explanation: COUNT tallies only the cells holding numbers, ignoring text and empty cells.
choice3: How many cells contain anything at all

description: What does =COUNTA(A1:A10) count that =COUNT(A1:A10) does not?
explanation: COUNTA counts every non-empty cell, including text, while COUNT only counts numbers.
choice3: Cells that are formatted in bold

description: Which symbol multiplies two values in a formula?
explanation: An asterisk is the multiplication operator in spreadsheet formulas.

description: Which symbol divides one value by another in a formula?
explanation: A forward slash is the division operator.

description: What does =A1^2 calculate?
explanation: The caret raises a value to a power, so this squares whatever is in A1.
choice3: The second character of A1

description: In =(A1+A2)*3, what do the brackets change?
explanation: Brackets force the addition to happen first, so the sum is multiplied by 3 rather than only A2.
choice1: They turn the result into text
choice2: They make the formula run faster
choice3: They make the addition happen before the multiplication

description: What happens to =A1 when you copy the formula one row down?
explanation: A plain reference is relative, so it shifts with the formula and becomes =A2.
choice3: It shows an error

description: What does the dollar sign do in a reference?
explanation: A dollar sign locks the part of the reference that follows it so it does not shift when the formula is copied.
choice0: Locks the row or column so it does not shift when copied
choice2: Marks the reference as pointing to another file
choice3: Turns the reference into text

description: Which reference stays pointing at exactly the same cell wherever it is copied?
explanation: Locking both the column and the row makes the reference fully absolute.

description: What does formatting a cell as a percentage do to the stored value 0.25?
explanation: Formatting changes only the display. The value stays 0.25 but is shown as 25 percent.
choice1: It shows 25 percent while the value stays 0.25
choice2: It multiplies the value by 100 permanently
choice3: It converts the value to text

description: Why might a cell show a row of hash marks instead of a number?
explanation: The column is too narrow to display the value, so widening the column reveals it.
choice3: The column is too narrow to show the value

description: What is the difference between deleting a row and hiding it?
explanation: Deleting removes the data permanently, while hiding only stops it being displayed.
choice0: Deleting removes the data, hiding only stops it being shown
choice1: They do exactly the same thing
choice2: Hiding removes the data, deleting only stops it being shown
choice3: Hiding works only on columns

description: What does the fill handle do when you drag it down a column?
explanation: Dragging the small square at the corner of a selection copies the cell or extends its pattern into the cells below.
choice0: Deletes the cells you drag over
choice2: Copies the cell or continues its pattern
choice3: Locks the cells you drag over

description: Why should a data table have a single header row?
explanation: A single header row names each column so sorting, filtering and lookups can identify the fields.
choice1: So each column has a name that features like sorting and filtering can use
choice2: Because formulas cannot read the first row
choice3: To stop the data being edited

description: What happens to your data when you sort only one column of a table?
explanation: Sorting one column alone moves its values while the other columns stay put, so the rows no longer line up.
hint: Think about whether the other columns move too.
choice0: The rows stop matching, because the other columns do not move
choice1: Nothing, the whole table always moves together
choice3: The sort is refused by the spreadsheet

description: What does a filter do to a list of data?
explanation: A filter temporarily hides the rows that do not match your criteria, leaving the data itself intact.
choice0: Deletes rows that do not match
choice1: Copies matching rows to a new sheet
choice3: Temporarily hides rows that do not match

description: What does =TODAY() return?
explanation: TODAY returns the current date, and it updates itself each time the sheet recalculates.
choice1: The date the file was created
choice2: The current date and time as text
choice3: The number of days in the month

description: What does =LEN("basket") return?
explanation: LEN counts the characters in a piece of text, and basket has 6.

description: What does =UPPER("total") return?
explanation: UPPER converts text to capital letters.
choice3: An error

description: What does the CONCATENATE function, or the & operator, do?
explanation: Both join pieces of text together into one string.
choice0: Joins pieces of text into one
choice3: Removes duplicate text

description: What does =ROUND(3.456, 1) return?
explanation: The second argument is the number of decimal places to keep, so 3.456 rounds to 3.5.

description: What does the error #DIV/0! mean?
explanation: The formula tried to divide by zero or by an empty cell.
choice1: The formula divided by zero or an empty cell
choice3: The value is too large to display

description: What does the error #NAME? usually mean?
explanation: The spreadsheet does not recognise something in the formula, most often a misspelled function name.
choice0: A function name is misspelled or unknown
choice1: The file has not been saved
choice2: Two sheets have the same name
choice3: A number was entered as text

description: What does the error #REF! mean?
explanation: The formula points at a cell that no longer exists, usually because its row, column or sheet was deleted.
choice2: The formula refers to a cell that no longer exists
choice3: Two formulas depend on each other

description: What does freezing the top row of a sheet do?
explanation: The frozen row stays visible while the rest of the sheet scrolls, keeping the headers in view.
choice1: Keeps the row visible while the rest scrolls
choice3: Copies the row to every sheet

description: What does the reference Sheet2!A1 mean?
explanation: An exclamation mark separates the sheet name from the cell, so this reads cell A1 on Sheet2.
choice0: Cell A1 on the sheet named Sheet2
choice1: The second cell in column A1
choice2: A warning attached to cell A1
choice3: Cell A1 copied into Sheet2

description: What is the difference between a workbook and a worksheet?
explanation: A workbook is the whole file; a worksheet is one grid of cells inside it.
choice2: A workbook is the file, a worksheet is one sheet inside it
choice3: A workbook can only ever hold one worksheet

description: Why does a number typed with a leading apostrophe behave differently?
explanation: The apostrophe forces the entry to be stored as text, so it will not take part in arithmetic.
choice0: It is stored as a negative number
choice1: It is rounded to the nearest whole number
choice3: It is stored as text rather than a number

description: What does =A1+A2+A3 do that =SUM(A1:A3) also does?
explanation: Both add the three cells. SUM is preferred because it survives inserting rows inside the range.
choice0: Both add the three values, but SUM adapts better to inserted rows
choice1: Only the first works with decimals
choice2: Only the second works with negative numbers
choice3: They give different totals

description: What appears in a cell if you type SUM(A1:A5) without the leading equals sign?
explanation: Without the equals sign the entry is not a formula, so the literal text is shown.
choice0: The total of A1 to A5
choice3: An empty cell

description: What is the safest way to keep the number 007 looking like 007?
explanation: Formatting the cell as text preserves the leading zeros, which a number format would strip.
choice2: Format the cell as text before typing
choice3: Type it as 7 and widen the column

description: What does =COUNTIF(A1:A10, ">5") return?
explanation: COUNTIF counts only the cells in the range that satisfy the condition, here values greater than 5.
choice0: How many cells hold a value greater than 5
choice1: The sum of the values greater than 5
choice3: How many cells hold exactly the text ">5"

description: What does =SUMIF(A1:A10, ">100") return?
explanation: SUMIF adds only the values in the range that meet the condition.
choice3: The total of the values over 100

description: What does conditional formatting do?
explanation: It changes how a cell looks based on rules about its value, for example shading negative numbers red.
choice0: Locks cells that meet a condition
choice1: Changes a cells appearance based on rules about its value
choice2: Hides cells that meet a condition
choice3: Converts values that meet a condition into text

description: What does merging cells do?
explanation: Merging combines several cells into one larger cell, which is useful for titles but often awkward for data tables.
choice0: Combines several cells into one larger cell
choice1: Adds the values of the cells together
choice2: Copies the first cell into all the others
choice3: Locks the cells against editing

description: Why is one record per row and one field per column the recommended layout?
explanation: This tabular shape is what sorting, filtering, lookups and pivot tables all expect.
choice1: It is the only layout that can be printed
choice2: Sorting, filtering, lookups and pivot tables all assume it
choice3: It prevents formulas from breaking when saved

description: What does =IF(A1>10, "high", "low") put in the cell?
explanation: IF tests the condition and returns the second argument when it is true and the third when it is false.
choice0: high when A1 is over 10, otherwise low
choice2: The value of A1 if it is over 10
choice3: TRUE or FALSE

description: What does pressing Ctrl and Z do?
explanation: Ctrl and Z undoes the most recent action.
choice3: Closes the workbook

description: What does it mean that a spreadsheet recalculates automatically?
explanation: When a cell changes, every formula that depends on it updates straight away without being re-entered.
choice0: The file saves itself at intervals
choice1: Formulas are converted to fixed values
choice2: Rounding is applied to every result
choice3: Dependent formulas update as soon as a value changes

description: What does setting a print area do?
explanation: It limits printing to the range you chose rather than the whole used sheet.
choice0: Prints only the range you selected
choice3: Fits the whole sheet onto one page

description: What is the difference between a value and a formula in a cell?
explanation: A value is typed data that stays as it is; a formula computes its result from other cells and updates when they change.
choice1: A formula can only hold text
choice2: A value is fixed, a formula computes a result that can change
choice3: A value updates automatically, a formula does not
